sources.citation: The Rosetta Project. 2010. Nomu Swadesh List (rosettaproject_noh_swadesh-1). archive.org
sources.note: 53-item wordlist (arm mɛtɛ, ashes kau, bone siwit..), no stress marks, no source note; forms match McElhanon & Voorhoeve 1970 per TransNewGuinea.org.

sources.citation: McElhanon, K. A. 1970. A history of linguistic research in the Huon Peninsula, New Guinea. PL C-13, 1178-1208. (ANU Open Research hdl 1885/253810)
sources.note: Research history; no Nomu-specific or stress content.

sources.citation: McElhanon, K. A. 1970. The Selepet language within the Finisterre-Huon phylum (New Guinea). PhD thesis, ANU. xi+477 leaves. (ANU Open Research hdl 1885/109875)
sources.note: Stress section (ch. 3 §5 'Stress group (word)': primary stress on the initial syllable, secondary on alternate syllables) is Selepet only; Nomu occurs solely in the Huon Peninsula classification lists (letter N). No Nomu phonology.

sources.citation: TransNewGuinea.org, Nomu language page (lexicon from McElhanon & Voorhoeve 1970)
sources.note: Only source listed for Nomu is McElhanon and Voorhoeve (1970); unstressed wordlist.

sources.citation: Suter, Edgar. 2018. Comparative Morphology of the Huon Peninsula Languages (Papua New Guinea). PhD dissertation, Universität zu Köln. viii+331 pp. (Glottolog ref 577703)
sources.note: Comparative morphology only ('the comparative phonology still awaits completion', Preface). p. 7: 'None of the three languages of this family [Dallman] has been the object of an in-depth study.. McElhanon as well as myself collected morphological and lexical data on Nomu'; p. 58: Nomu data = McElhanon's 1968 survey + Suter's 1996 object-verb elicitation. The only stress/accent remarks are historical-comparative conjectures about Proto-Western-Huon suffixes being unstressed (the text) and Selepet/Kâte word accent (lines 7363-7368, p. 250); nothing on Nomu word stress.

sources.citation: Pawley, Andrew & Harald Hammarström. 2017. The Trans New Guinea family. In Bill Palmer (ed.), The Languages and Linguistics of the New Guinea Area: A Comprehensive Guide, 21-195. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. (OAPEN open chapter; archive.org id oapen-20.500.12657-23719)
sources.note: Nothing on Nomu. Family-level remark only (after Ross 2005): 'In languages of the Madang and Finisterre-Huon groups and of South-east Papua generally, tone and pitch accent are largely absent.' Confirms best documentation known for Nomu in 2017 was Smith 1988's numerals.

sources.citation: Hammarström, Harald & Sebastian Nordhoff. 2012. Online appendix to 'The languages of Melanesia: quantifying the level of coverage'. In N. Evans & M. Klamer (eds), Melanesian languages on the edge of Asia (LD&C Special Publication 5), 13-34. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press.
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: coverage inventory only: entry lists Smith 1988 only; no stress/tone statement (database of descriptive coverage, not a description)

sources.citation: Suter, Edgar. 2012. Verbs with pronominal object prefixes in Finisterre-Huon languages. In Harald Hammarström & Wilco van den Heuvel (eds), History, contact and classification of Papuan languages (Language & Linguistics in Melanesia, Special Issue 2012, Part I), 23-58.
sources.note: No phonology of Nomu. The only stress remarks (p. 37) concern Somba: pHP *a > Somba /i/ 'in the unstressed second syllable of words whereas it becomes /e/ in the stressed first syllable' — a historical argument about Somba, not Nomu. Nomu forms are given without stress marks.

sources.citation: SIL Papua New Guinea. 2007-2013. PNG Language Resources: Nomu [noh] (www-01.sil.org/pacific/png/show_lang_entry.asp?id=noh) and PNG Bibliography of published and unpublished works, language index. Internet Archive captures of 2015.
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: No content: 'Language resources: Nothing yet available or materials are not yet processed.' Nomu is also absent from the SIL PNG Bibliography language index (which includes unpublished manuscripts), so no SIL survey, wordlist or Organised Phonology Data exists for Nomu.

sources.citation: Suter, Edgar. 1997. A comparative look at the dual and plural forms of verb inflections and pronouns in Northeast New Guinea Papuan languages. Language and Linguistics in Melanesia 28: 17-68.
sources.note: Morphology (dual/plural consonant alternation) only in the pages read; no phonology or prosody content for Nomu expected or seen.

sources.citation: Smith, Geoffrey P. 1988. Morobe counting systems. Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 26 (PL A-76), 1-132. (Glottolog ref 8921; ANU Open Research hdl 1885/253560)
sources.note: §56 Nomu (p. 83): numerals 1-20 from a high-school student (wetku, okop, okop so wetku, mete wetku..). Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: McElhanon, K. A. 1984. A linguistic field guide to the Morobe Province, Papua New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics D-57. (ANU Open Research hdl 1885/145233)
sources.note: Village gazetteer (Ezanko, Gitukia, Sikikia listed as Nomu villages). Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: McElhanon, K. A. 1975. North-Eastern Trans-New Guinea Phylum languages. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 1 (PL C-38), 527-567. (ANU Open Research hdl 1885/252970)
sources.note: Survey/classification chapter. §2.8.1.3.3.3 Nomu (WH-10), p. 535: pop. 810; 'In 1968 informants indicated to the present writer that the Nomu language became extinct about 1900. Data collected at that time revealed ONO roots with NOMU affixation. More recent comments, however, indicate that there may yet be some Nomu speakers alive.' No stress statement (0 hits).

sources.citation: McElhanon, K. A. 1973. Towards a typology of the Finisterre-Huon languages, New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics B-22. Canberra: ANU. viii+80 pp. (ANU Open Research hdl 1885/145136)
sources.harvard_location: Divinity School Library (offsite storage), call number - Ask at Circulation (Pamph. folio) BS 354 .Z91
sources.note: Ch. 1 Phonology (pp. 5-7: phonemes, syllable structure, morphophonemics) compares ten representative languages (Rawa, Wantoat, Uri, Kewieng, Kube, Kâte, Kovai, Nabak, Selepet..), not Nomu; Nomu appears only in the classification list (p. vii). No mention of stress or accent anywhere in the book (de-spaced scanned a full-text search for stress/accent found nothing).

sources.citation: Hooley, B. A. & K. A. McElhanon. 1970. Languages of the Morobe District, New Guinea. In Wurm & Laycock (eds), Pacific linguistic studies in honour of Arthur Capell (PL C-13), 1065-1094. (ANU Open Research hdl 1885/253805)
sources.note: Lexicostatistical classification. Nomu: 50% cognate with Ono, non-basic vocabulary largely replaced by Ono forms; 'Informants indicate that the aboriginal speakers of Nomu died out about the time of initial European contact.' Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: McElhanon, K. A. & C. L. Voorhoeve. 1970. The Trans-New Guinea Phylum: explorations in deep-level genetic relationships. Pacific Linguistics B-16. (ANU Open Research hdl 1885/146444)
sources.note: Source of the Nomu wordlist used by TransNewGuinea.org/Rosetta; Nomu appears only in the classification list (Western Huon Family e.). No stress marking, no stress statement.
